name: investor-tells
of: A mechanism by which a founder reads an investor's real position, where the decision sits, what stage the process is in, what the fund can do, and whose politics govern it, off something the investor spends, forgoes, sequences, or signs rather than says, named with the carrier read, the state it reveals, and the case where it lies, and sorted by where the founder must stand to see it: in the public record before contact, in the room, in the following week, in the diligence, on the paper, in a move the founder must make, or only after the wire.
items: Ledger's clock: whether a yes is even available is read from the fund's own deployment record before the partner's appetite matters, since a fund in year four of a five-year investment period with half its capital uncalled must deploy and a fund that made nine investments in its first year and one in its third is holding reserves for its own portfolio, and both are visible in announced checks and filing dates before the first email; the carrier is the fund's ledger and not the partner, and it lies when the visible fund is not the vehicle that would write this check, an unannounced successor fund or an opportunity vehicle running on a different clock.

Partner's name on the door: whether the person across the table can carry a deal is read from whose name sits on the fund's last deals, its board seats and its announcements, not from the title on the website, since a venture partner, a principal, or an operating partner can refer but cannot spend; it lies in exactly one case, the newly made partner whose name is on nothing because their first deal is still to come, and who therefore has the strongest motive in the building to close one.

Neighbor in the portfolio: if the fund already holds a company in the founder's market, the meeting's purpose is set before it starts, and the tell is whether the partner names the neighbor unprompted, since an undisclosed neighbor makes the meeting intelligence gathered for it; it adds to cooperative-masks' alliance proposed to inventory your capabilities the check that can be run from the portfolio page before the alliance is proposed, and it lies at a fund that runs an index strategy and will honestly own two rivals, which its ledger shows as other such pairs.

Second body: partner attention is the fund's scarcest unit, so a second partner at the second meeting means the first has spent standing inside the partnership to bring one, as a medieval charter's witness list tells a historian which magnates the king needed present, while an associate-only follow-up, however warm, is still screening; a partner who writes the follow-up in their own words at midnight but cannot bring a second body is appetite without a vote, and the tell lies at a fund of two partners, where every meeting is a partner meeting and the reading must fall back to whether the meeting was moved to the founder's site.

Who sums up: the partnership's internal rank is read in the room from who interrupts whom and who restates the deal at the end, since the one who summarizes holds the pen the others will read from on Monday, the way a newcomer in a prison yard reads rank not from size but from who is deferred to; not who came, which is Second body, but the order of speech among those who did, and it lies at partnerships that perform equality, where the reading falls back to whom the others ask the last question.

Queue interval: an interval the founder is made to wait measures this deal's rank in a queue the founder cannot see, so the days before the second meeting read the partner's queue against whatever else that partner saw this week, and after signing the days before counsel returns a standard document read the fund's closing queue and whether it is waiting on something unsaid, a co-investor, a consent, a successor fund; it adds to lead-time-floors' Partner meeting, which reads what the calendar does to the founder's runway, by reading what the interval says about the investor's ordering, and it lies whenever the interval is the fund's clock rather than the partner's, in August, in December, or under must-deploy, which is why a fast second meeting from a fund late in its period reads the ledger and not the partner.

Tense switch: an investor still deciding asks about the past, why the cohort churned, why this architecture, while an investor who has decided asks about the deal, round size, who else is in, whether there is room to lead, and the switch usually precedes any spoken yes by days; the sharpest form is the allocation question, how much can we take, which is addressed to the other investors through the founder, as an auction bidder who asks about the reserve has stopped inspecting the lot; it lies when a partner asks round size first to check the fund's check-size fit, which is a size question and not an allocation question.

Borrowed eyes: an investor whose first question is who else is in holds a position that is a function of another investor's, so the founder is reading the wrong node and every later tell from this investor should be re-read as a tell about the lead it follows, a day late; it lies when the question is about round mechanics from a fund that never leads and honestly needs a lead to set terms, which its ledger shows as a record of follows.

Holdable sentence: an investor's words are read by whether they could later be quoted back against the speaker, so we would love to see more traction is a pass that keeps a free option on the company, while at this revenue with this retention, call me and we move in a week binds a metric, a threshold, and a date, as an employer who names a wage reopener date has conceded something and one who says we will look at it next year has not; the carrier is the cost of being quoted, and it lies when a fund rule such as a stage floor makes the vagueness honest rather than option-keeping, which is checked against the ledger.

Named objection: a no that states the specific objection that won reveals that a vote happened and the sponsor argued and lost, since only someone who fought the objection can name it exactly, while a no attributed to the partnership in generic terms reveals that the deal never reached the room; it adds to deal-deaths' Champion's single-tender want, which reads how a sponsor's leaving kills a deal, by reading from the wording of the no whether a sponsor existed at all, and it lies when a partner who killed the deal alone reads back the founder's own weakest slide as the objection.

Order of asks: a request for the data room before a partner-meeting date has been set reverses the usual order, in which a partner buys in, the partnership authorizes the work, and the room is opened, so it reads a partner who lacks standing and needs the data to win the room, or a fund whose associates screen on numbers before any partner looks; it is preparation rather than screening only when the ask arrives with a date attached, and it lies at growth funds where quantitative screening precedes every partner by design.

Shopping list: diligence questions divide by whether the answer is useful to someone other than the decider, so named customers with prices, a pipeline by account, and a roadmap by quarter are transferable to a portfolio company while the reason a cohort churned is not, and the test is whether the investor accepts anonymized accounts and founder-chosen reference names, since a decider needs the shape and a shopper needs the names; it lies at late-stage funds whose cohort work needs account-level data, separated by their willingness to route it through a third-party quality-of-earnings firm that returns only the shape.

Back-channel spent: a call to a reference the founder offered is process, but a call to someone the founder did not offer, a former employee, a former investor, a rival's founder, costs the caller a favor and is spent only near the decision, so learning of it, usually from the person called, reads that the partner meeting is close and names the objection being tested; the reverse of lead-time-floors' Seeking is telling, since here the investor's search is visible to the founder, and the sharper reading is the call not made, because a term sheet issued with no back-channel is a reservation and not a decision; it lies at large multi-stage funds whose research staff call everyone at screen, where the favor costs the partner nothing.

Fuse length: the expiry on a term sheet is priced against when the investor expects a rival sheet to arrive, so a short fuse reveals the investor's own estimate that the founder's alternatives are good, an outside estimate of the founder's price carried by the party who will pay it, as a kidnapper's deadline reveals what the kidnapper believes the family can raise by then; it also reads the fund's clock when the close-by date is the fund's own, and it lies at funds that put a fuse on every sheet as house style, which founders who took their paper can tell you and which only Let it lapse can test.

Exclusivity as confession: the length of the no-shop the investor asks for measures the work the investor has not yet done and the room to walk it wants to keep, so sixty days from a fund that has spent no back-channel is an option and ten days from one that has is a close; it adds to lead-time-floors' No-shop, which reads what the lock does to the founder's clock, by reading what the lock's length says about the investor's remaining doubt, and it lies where the length was set by counsel's template rather than by the partner.

Term as forecast: each protective term is a bet on a future state, so the redline shows the investor's private forecast, a participating preference pricing a middling exit as likely, a full ratchet pricing a down round, super pro-rata pricing a wish for more, information rights without a seat pricing a passive hold, as an arms treaty's inspection clauses name the breach each side expects; only deviations from the fund's standard paper read, since house paper forecasts nothing, and the founder learns the standard from other founders who took it; it lies where the partner has not read what counsel sent.

Let it lapse: some tells exist only if the founder moves, so an expiry allowed to pass by a day reads whether the fuse was real, since a re-issued sheet shows the investor feared losing the deal more than being seen to bluff and a withdrawn one shows the clock was the fund's, as a deadline a kidnapper lets pass unacted reveals the deadline was a bluff; likewise offering anonymized accounts reads the shopper and declining the early data room reads whether a partner date appears; not a tell observed but a probe run, at the price of being wrong once, and it lies when the counterparty is not a partner but a committee that records the lapse as a fact.

Next-round hand: the investor's position is finally read after the wire, at the next round, in whether the fund takes its pro-rata, bridges a gap, or lets another lead mark the company down, which arrives too late for this raise and is the first tell for the next founder, because a fund's last three checks and its follow-ons are exactly the post-wire hands that other founders could not use in time, so the outside-readable ledger is made of other people's late tells; it lies when the fund's reserves ran out for reasons of vintage rather than belief, which Ledger's clock separates.

source.register: Operator-grade and concrete: partner hours, witness lists, filing dates, expiry clauses, no-shop lengths, anonymized customer lists, pro-rata; drawn from venture practice, medieval diplomatics, hostage negotiation, labor bargaining, auctions, and arms treaties.
source.mode: Analytical distinctions with composite observed cases; the thesis that every tell lies through its denominator is the author's analytical claim and is marked as such; Fuse length's reading of the founder's own price and Next-round hand's loop through other founders are speculative-analytical, kept with their modality visible.
source.via: practice-deep-ideonomy; two Fable fieldwork breaths; independent Fable editorial review
boundary_claim: Authored analytical fieldwork from composite cases in venture practice; no item is a documented history of any named fund, and the remote cases (charter witness lists, kidnappers' deadlines, treaty inspection clauses, wage reopeners) are simplified to expose one mechanism each.

The seriation is an itinerary of where the founder must stand to see the carrier, not a ranking of reliability or importance; a tell late on the route is not a better tell, and map edges are conditional authored claims.

Every tell is read against a denominator, the fund's size, age, decision rule, and the partner's tenure, which the map treats as readable from the ledger; where the ledger is private, an unannounced vehicle or a family office, the readings above are undefined, and the map does not claim the ledger is always public.

Tells about the investor's future conduct, how they behave in a down round or whom they let the founder call, are outside the item type except at Next-round hand, where past conduct becomes the next founder's ledger; the map reads position, not character.

The map reads the investor and does not say what the founder should do with the reading; tells the investor can fake cheaply once the map is known, a second body sent as theater, a fuse set for show, are named as lies inside items but are not mapped as a class.

seriation.axis: Where the founder must stand for the carrier to be visible, and whether seeing it requires the founder to move: from the public record read before the first email (Ledger's clock), through the room, the following week, the diligence, and the paper, to a probe the founder must run (Let it lapse), and finally to the next round after the wire (Next-round hand), where the tell arrives too late for this raise.
seriation.note: An authored itinerary of residence, not a ranking of reliability; the tells readable from outside in a week are the first nine, the ledger, the room, the interval, the tense, and the holdable sentence, and the paper's tells are clocks and forecasts. The hinge adjacency is Back-channel spent → Fuse length: the last tell readable before paper and the first readable on it, and the adjacency teaches that a term sheet is a different object depending on whether the back-channel preceded it, a reservation that freezes the founder's alternatives or a decision that prices them. Let it lapse sits after the paper and before the wire because it is the only station where the founder is not a reader but an actor; Next-round hand closes the route because nothing later can be read for this raise, and its edge back to Ledger's clock says the route is a loop through other founders.

exploration.first_question: What does an investor do, rather than say, that reveals where their decision actually sits, and which of those doings can a founder read from outside in a week and which only after a term sheet?
exploration.changed_question: What must the founder know about the investor's cost of each carrier before any behavior becomes a reading at all? Sharpening each item's lie case in breath one produced the same shape every time: the tell lies where the carrier is cheap or dear for that investor for reasons unrelated to this deal, a two-partner fund where a second body costs nothing, a fund late in its period where speed is the ledger's, a house template where the fuse is nobody's. So the question became one about denominators, and it turned up tells whose reading transfers to another node (Borrowed eyes), tells that exist only if the founder moves (Let it lapse), and the tell that arrives too late and becomes the next founder's ledger (Next-round hand), which closed the route into a loop the first framing had drawn as a line.
exploration.new_member: Let it lapse: some tells exist only if the founder moves, so an expiry allowed to pass by a day reads whether the fuse was real, since a re-issued sheet shows the investor feared losing the deal more than being seen to bluff and a withdrawn one shows the clock was the fund's, as a deadline a kidnapper lets pass unacted reveals the deadline was a bluff; likewise offering anonymized accounts reads the shopper and declining the early data room reads whether a partner date appears; not a tell observed but a probe run, at the price of being wrong once, and it lies when the counterparty is not a partner but a committee that records the lapse as a fact.

priorities.item: Holdable sentence: an investor's words are read by whether they could later be quoted back against the speaker, so we would love to see more traction is a pass that keeps a free option on the company, while at this revenue with this retention, call me and we move in a week binds a metric, a threshold, and a date, as an employer who names a wage reopener date has conceded something and one who says we will look at it next year has not; the carrier is the cost of being quoted, and it lies when a fund rule such as a stage floor makes the vagueness honest rather than option-keeping, which is checked against the ledger.
priorities.why: It is the cheapest tell on the route, read from the wording of passes the founder already holds, and if quotability predicts later conversion it turns every pass into a sorted follow-up list rather than a pile.
priorities.next_question: Take the passes received in one raise and sort each by whether it names a metric, a threshold, and a date; at the next raise, re-approach both sorted sets with the same update and record which set converts to a meeting within a week, to learn whether the holdable pass predicts a later yes or is merely a politer no.

priorities.item: Next-round hand: the investor's position is finally read after the wire, at the next round, in whether the fund takes its pro-rata, bridges a gap, or lets another lead mark the company down, which arrives too late for this raise and is the first tell for the next founder, because a fund's last three checks and its follow-ons are exactly the post-wire hands that other founders could not use in time, so the outside-readable ledger is made of other people's late tells; it lies when the fund's reserves ran out for reasons of vintage rather than belief, which Ledger's clock separates.
priorities.why: Low plausibility that any week-one tell predicts the post-wire hand, high generative promise: if one does, the loop back to Ledger's clock becomes a way to read a fund's future conduct from other founders' first meetings, and if none does, the map's outside-readable half is honestly severed from what it most wants to know.
priorities.next_question: For one fund, list its portfolio's next rounds over three years and mark where it took pro-rata, bridged, or let another lead mark the company down; then ask those founders what the partner did in the first two weeks (second body, tense switch, back-channel) and see whether any week-one tell sorts the hands better than the fund's vintage does.

gate.standard: declared type, close-neighbor discriminator, boundary case, and form inference

neighbors.left: Fuse length: the expiry on a term sheet is priced against when the investor expects a rival sheet to arrive, so a short fuse reveals the investor's own estimate that the founder's alternatives are good, an outside estimate of the founder's price carried by the party who will pay it, as a kidnapper's deadline reveals what the kidnapper believes the family can raise by then; it also reads the fund's clock when the close-by date is the fund's own, and it lies at funds that put a fuse on every sheet as house style, which founders who took their paper can tell you and which only Let it lapse can test.
neighbors.right: Exclusivity as confession: the length of the no-shop the investor asks for measures the work the investor has not yet done and the room to walk it wants to keep, so sixty days from a fund that has spent no back-channel is an option and ten days from one that has is a close; it adds to lead-time-floors' No-shop, which reads what the lock does to the founder's clock, by reading what the lock's length says about the investor's remaining doubt, and it lies where the length was set by counsel's template rather than by the partner.
neighbors.separating_case: A sheet with a forty-eight-hour fuse and a sixty-day no-shop: the fuse says the investor fears a rival sheet this week, the no-shop says the investor has not decided, and together they read an investor trying to freeze the market before doing the work; a sheet with a ten-day fuse and a ten-day no-shop is the opposite object, an investor who has decided and fears nobody. The two clocks read two different states, the investor's estimate of the founder's alternatives and the investor's own remaining doubt, and can point in opposite directions on one page.

checks.boundary_case: Which founders the investor lets you call is a tempting nonmember: it is read from what the investor does rather than says, but it reads how the investor will behave after the wire, their conduct in a down round, not where their decision on this deal sits, so it is out of type. Next-round hand is in on exactly that contrast, since it reads the fund's position (reserves, belief) at the point where past conduct becomes another founder's ledger.
checks.form_inference: The map shows a loop the sequence conceals: Next-round hand → Ledger's clock, where the last tell of one raise, unusable in time, is the first tell of the next founder's, so the outside-readable half of the route is made of other founders' late tells. It shows a dependency, Ledger's clock → Queue interval and Partner's name on the door → Second body, where a behavior has no reading until its denominator has been read. It shows a fork, Back-channel spent → Fuse length, where the same expiry clause is a reservation or a decision depending on what preceded it. It shows a passage between nodes, Borrowed eyes → Tense switch, where the reading transfers to a different investor and this one's tells are discarded. And it shows a passage between levels, Let it lapse → Fuse length, from observation to experiment, where a tell has no settled reading until the founder acts.
checks.target_preserved: Self-read only. Each admitted item names a distinct carrier, a distinct state it reveals, and a distinct case where it lies; the strange members (a tell that reads the founder's own price off the investor's fear, a tell that transfers to another node, a tell that exists only if the founder moves, a tell that arrives too late and becomes someone else's first tell) are kept as mechanisms rather than softened into a list of red flags.
